DETAILED ACTION
Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Information Disclosure Statement
The information disclosure statement (IDS) submitted on 07 November 2019 is in compliance with the provisions of 37 CFR 1.97. Accordingly, the information disclosure statements is being considered by the examiner.
Claim Objections
Claims 32 and 36 are objected to because of the following informalities:
Claim 32 recites “further comprising the step of:” when it should most likely recite “further comprising the steps of:”.
Claim 36 recites “The method of claim 23” when it should most likely recite “The method of claim 32”. If this is not the case, claim 36 would be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) for being indefinite because acceleration is not mentioned in any previous claim that claim 36 depends on.
Appropriate correction is required.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b)  CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
Claims 32-33 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA  the applicant regards as the invention.
Claim 32 recites the limitation “the retrieved delta values” in line 2 of the claim.  There is insufficient antecedent basis for this limitation in the claim.
Claim 33 recites the limitation “the group of nutritional information” in line 3 of the claim.  There is insufficient antecedent basis for this limitation in the claim.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
In the event the determination of the status of the application as subject to AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 (or as subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 102 and 103) is incorrect, any correction of the statutory basis for the rejection will not be considered a new ground of rejection if the prior art relied upon, and the rationale supporting the rejection, would be the same under either status.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
Claims 21-25, and 28 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over U.S. 2002/0143262 to Bardy in view of U.S. 2017/0007153 to Tonar et al. further in view of U.S. 2011/0191122 to Kharraz Tavakol et al.
As per claim 21, Bardy teaches a method of providing a continuity of care for a patient during transfer from a first care setting to a second care setting, the method comprising the steps of:
--making a plurality of measurements at a body location on the patient at the second care setting, (see: paragraph [0009] where information about the patient is constantly being recorded by an external or implantable medical device. These measurements are being recorded regardless of location, thus it can be considered recording these measurements at a second care setting)
--determining whether the value exceeds a threshold, (see: paragraph [0093] where patient status values are being determined to either stay within or cross a certain SD threshold)
--continuing to administer the current intervention if the value does not exceed the threshold, (see: paragraph [0093] where if the patient status indicates status quo, then no changes in treatment or diagnosis are indicated) and
--administering a new intervention of level-N if the value exceeds the threshold, where N has a value greater than K (see: paragraph [0093] where a slightly more aggressive diagnostic, and if appropriate, treatment program is undertaken for a more rapidly deteriorating condition where a change of 1.0 SD has occurred over the course of about 1 week. A new intervention of level-N (aggressive diagnostic treatment program) is being administered if the value (change away from status  quo value in SD) exceeds a threshold (SD threshold). N here has a value greater than K because the N treatment (aggressive diagnostic treatment program) is greater than the K treatment (base level treatment). Also see: paragraph [0092]).
Bardy teaches the aforementioned claim limitations. The difference between Bardy and the claimed invention is that while Bardy does disclose measurement values and values that are being compared to thresholds to determine if therapy needs to change, it does not explicitly teach SEM measurements, calculating a delta value, and determining if that delta value exceeds a threshold.
Bardy fails to specifically teach:
1) --identifying a current intervention of level-K received by the patient at the first care setting;
2) --Sub-Epidermal Moisture (SEM) measurements,
3) --calculating a delta value by a difference between two of the plurality of SEM measurements, and
4) --delta value as a value.
Tonar et al. teaches:
2) --Sub-Epidermal Moisture (SEM) measurements, (see: paragraph [0008] where there are SEM values)
3) --calculating a delta value by a difference between two of the plurality of SEM measurements, (see: paragraph [0008] where a difference between a max SEM value and min SEM value is determined) and
4) --delta value as a value (see: paragraph [0008] where a difference value (delta value) is being determined).
Therefore it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to substitute 2) Sub-Epidermal Moisture (SEM) measurements, 3) calculate a delta value by a difference between two of the plurality of SEM measurements, and have the 4) delta value as a value as taught by Tonar et al. for myocardial ischemia measurements and myocardial ischemia threshold values as disclosed by Bardy since each individual element and its function are shown in the prior art, with the difference being the substitution of the elements. In the present case, Bardy determines if values reach a certain threshold and then administers a new intervention for myocardial ischemia. Bardy is determining this intervention using measured body values, thus substituting the type of values from myocardial ischemia to SEM where SEM values are also body measurement values would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art. Thus, one of ordinary skill in the art could have substituted the one known element for the other to produce a predictable result (MPEP 2143).
Kharraz Tavakol et al. teaches:
1) --identifying a current intervention of level-K received by the patient at the first care setting (see: paragraph [0013] where a patient’s medical history is being transferred from one setting to another. Also see: paragraph [0018] where patient’s progress after a treatment can be tracked allowing for a more effective treatment in the next patient-doctor meeting. A current intervention of level-K (medical history of the patient which includes the treatments performed on the patient) is being identified in this transferred information).
One of ordinary skill at the time of the invention was filed would have found it obvious to 1) identify a current intervention of level-K received by the patient at the first care setting as taught by Kharraz Tavakol et al. in the method as taught by Bardy and Tonar et al. in combination with the motivation(s) of preventing delays in medical care and preventing patient dissuasion from treatment protocol compliance (see: paragraph [0002] of Kharraz Tavakol et al.).
As per claim 22, Bardy, Tonar et al., and Kharraz Tavakol et al. in combination teach the method of claim 21, see discussion of claim 21. Kharraz Tavakol et al. further teaches wherein the current intervention of level-K is provided in a transfer record (see: paragraphs [0013] and [0018] where the patient’s information that is being transferred is considered to be a transfer record).
The motivations to combine the above-mentioned references are discussed in the rejection of claim 21, and incorporated herein.
As per claim 23, Bardy, Tonar et al., and Kharraz Tavakol et al. in combination teach the method of claim 22, see discussion of claim 22. Bardy teaches values taken at different times while in the first care setting (see: paragraph [0009] where measures are being collected on a regular, periodic basis for storage in a database. There are multiple data/measurement sets being recorded here periodically (at different times) at a particular setting).
Tonar et al. teaches delta values calculated from a portion of the plurality of SEM scans of the patient (see: paragraph [0008] where a difference value (delta value) is  being determined. The plural scans and values aspect here was taught by Bardy. The calculation for a single delta value on a scan here is being taught into Bardy where multiple values are being recorded periodically).
Kharraz Tavakol et al. teaches the transfer record further comprises values (see: paragraphs [0013] and [0018] where the patient’s information that is being transferred is considered to be a transfer record. The patient’s past information and medical history (specific values) are within the transfer record (the patient’s information that is transferred)).
The motivations to combine the above-mentioned references are discussed in the rejection of claim 21, and incorporated herein.
As per claim 24, Bardy, Tonar et al., and Kharraz Tavakol et al. in combination teach the method of claim 22, see discussion of claim 22. Kharraz Tavakol et al. further teaches wherein the transfer record further comprises results obtained from at least one of assessments (see: paragraphs [0013] and [0018] where there is patient’s information including medical history being transferred to another office electronically).
Tonar et al. teaches assessments selected from the group consisting of a risk assessment of the patient, a visual skin assessment of at least one body location of the patient, and an image of the at least one body location (see: FIGS 9A and 9B where there is a result of a visual representation (SEM measurement map of damaged tissue) of at least one body location of the patient).
The motivations to combine the above-mentioned references are discussed in the rejection of claim 21, and incorporated herein.
As per claim 25, Bardy, Tonar et al., and Kharraz Tavakol et al. in combination teach the method of claim 22, see discussion of claim 22. Tonar et al. further teaches wherein the record further comprises results obtained from performing a first SEM scan of at least one body location of the patient while in the first care setting, wherein the first SEM scan comprises a plurality of measurements of an SEM value at the body location and calculation of a first delta value from the plurality of SEM values (see: FIGS 9A and 9B where there is a SEM measurement map (scan) of damaged tissue of at least one body location of the patient. This scan contains a plurality of SEM values at the body location of sternum. Also see: paragraph [0008] where there is a difference (delta) being calculated with the scan between a max and min SEM value).
Kharraz Tavakol et al. teaches a transfer record as a record, (see: paragraphs [0013] and [0018] where the patient’s information being transferred is the transfer record) and wherein said transfer record is stored on a database (see: paragraphs [0117] and [0128]).
The motivations to combine the above-mentioned references are discussed in the rejection of claim 21, and incorporated herein.
As per claim 28, Bardy, Tonar et al., and Kharraz Tavakol et al. in combination teach the method of claim 21, see discussion of claim 21. Tonar et al. further teaches  wherein said delta value is calculated by a difference between a maximum SEM measurement and a minimum SEM measurement selected from the plurality of SEM measurements (see: paragraph [0008] where a difference between a max SEM value and min SEM value is determined).
The motivations to combine the above-mentioned references are discussed in the rejection of claim 21, and incorporated herein.
Claims 26, 29-30, and 37-38 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over U.S. 2002/0143262 to Bardy in view of U.S. 2017/0007153 to Tonar et al. further in view of U.S. 2011/0191122 to Kharraz Tavakol et al. as applied to claim 21, and further in view of U.S. Patent No. 6,738,798 to Ploetz et al.
As per claim 26, Bardy, Tonar et al., and Kharraz Tavakol et al. in combination teach the method of claim 25, see discussion of claim 25. Tonar et al. teaches SEM scan (see: FIG. 4 and paragraph [0008]).
Kharraz Tavakol et al. further teaches wherein: the transfer record further comprises a patient identifier (see: paragraphs [0036] and [0037] where the database includes an identifier for correlating patient and patient records).
The combination fails to specifically, further teach that the record further comprises a date and a time when said first scan was performed.
Ploetz et al. teaches that the record further comprises a date and a time when said first scan was performed (see: column 4, line 48 to column 5, line 13 where there is exam data including exam date and start/end time and this information is collected by the automated support central server).
One of ordinary skill at the time of the invention was filed would have found it obvious to have the record further comprises a date and a time when said first scan was performed as taught by Ploetz et al. in the method as taught by Bardy, Tonar et al., and Kharraz Tavakol et al. in combination with the motivation(s) of providing accurate and detailed records of the health status of a patient.
As per claim 29, Bardy, Tonar et al., Kharraz Tavakol et al., and Ploetz et al. in combination teach the method of claim 26, see discussion of claim 26. Bardy further teaches further comprising the steps of:
--performing measurements of the body location of the patient in the second care setting to obtain a second plurality of SEM measurements (see: paragraph [0009] where information about the patient is constantly being recorded by an external or implantable medical device. These measurements are being recorded regardless of location, thus it can be considered recording these measurements at a second care setting. A second plurality of measurements occurs after the first set of measurements are taken because the patient is constantly being recorded) and
--reporting the second data record to the database (see: paragraph [0009] where measures are being collected on a regular, periodic basis for storage in a database. The second data record would include the measures that were taken after a first set of measures during the periodic collection of measures) and
--second set of measurements and data (see: paragraph [0009] where measures are being collected on a regular, periodic basis for storage in a  database. There are multiple data/measurement sets being recorded here periodically including a second set).
Tonar et al. teaches:
--measurements as a SEM scan, (see: FIG. 4 and paragraph [0008])
--calculating a delta value, (see: paragraph [0008] where a difference between a max SEM value and min SEM value is determined)
--creating a data record that comprises the delta value, (see: paragraph [0008] where there is a difference (delta) being calculated with the scan between a max and min SEM value and this value is part of the record of the patient) and
--SEM scan (see: FIG. 4 and paragraph [0008]).
Kharraz Tavakol et al. teaches:
--creating a data record that comprises the patient identifier (see: paragraphs [0036] and [0037] where the database includes an identifier for correlating patient and patient records).
The motivations to combine the above-mentioned references are discussed in the rejection of claim 21, and incorporated herein.
Ploetz et al. teaches:
--creating a data record that comprises a date and time when the scan was performed (see: column 4, line 48 to column 5, line 13 where there is exam data including exam date and start/end time and this information is collected by the automated support central server).
The motivations to combine the above-mentioned references are discussed in the rejection of claim 26, and incorporated herein.
As per claim 30, Bardy, Tonar et al., Kharraz Tavakol et al., and Ploetz et al. in combination teach the method of claim 29, see discussion of claim 29. Bardy teaches second set of measurements and data (see: paragraph [0009] where measures are being collected on a regular, periodic basis for storage in a database. There are multiple data/measurement sets being recorded here periodically including a second set).
Tonar et al. further teaches wherein said delta value is calculated by a difference between a maximum SEM measurement and a minimum SEM measurement selected from the plurality of SEM measurements (see: paragraph [0008] where a difference between a max SEM value and min SEM value is determined).
The motivations to combine the above-mentioned references are discussed in the rejection of claim 21, and incorporated herein.
As per claim 37, Bardy, Tonar et al., Kharraz Tavakol et al., and Ploetz et al. in combination teach the method of claim 29, see discussion of claim 29. Bardy further teaches further comprising the steps of:
--performing measurements of the body location of the patient in the second care setting to obtain a third plurality of SEM measurements (see: paragraph [0009] where information about the patient is constantly being recorded by an external or implantable medical device. These measurements are being recorded regardless of location, thus it can be considered recording these measurements at a second number='10'care setting. A third plurality of measurements occurs after the second set of measurements are taken because the patient is constantly being recorded) and
--reporting the third data record to the database (see: paragraph [0009] where measures are being collected on a regular, periodic basis for storage in a database. The second data record would include the measures that were taken after a first set of measures during the periodic collection of measures) and
--third set of measurements and data (see: paragraph [0009] where measures are being collected on a regular, periodic basis for storage in a database. There are multiple data/measurement sets being recorded here periodically including a third set).
Tonar et al. teaches:
--measurements as a SEM scan, (see: FIG. 4 and paragraph [0008])
--calculating a delta value, (see: paragraph [0008] where a difference between a max SEM value and min SEM value is determined)
--creating a data record that comprises the delta value, (see: paragraph [0008] where there is a difference (delta) being calculated with the scan between a max and min SEM value and this value is part of the record of the patient) and
--SEM scan (see: FIG. 4 and paragraph [0008]).
Kharraz Tavakol et al. teaches:
--creating a data record that comprises the patient identifier (see: paragraphs [0036] and [0037] where the database includes an identifier for correlating patient and patient records).

Ploetz et al. teaches:
--creating a data record that comprises a date and time when the scan was performed (see: column 4, line 48 to column 5, line 13 where there is exam data including exam date and start/end time and this information is collected by the automated support central server).
The motivations to combine the above-mentioned references are discussed in the rejection of claim 26, and incorporated herein.
Additionally, claim limitations of claim 37 recite limitations similar to claim limitations already stated within claim 29 without adding any other functionalities. Repeating steps that do not add a new and unexpected result has no patentable significance (see: MPEP 2144.04 (VI)(B), Duplication of Parts). Simply repeating steps that were applied to one set of questions and applying those steps to another set of questions produces expected results, and as such, amounts to a mere duplication of parts conferring to no additional patentable weight.
As per claim 38, Bardy, Tonar et al., Kharraz Tavakol et al., and Ploetz et al. in combination teach the method of claim 37, see discussion of claim 37. There are multiple data/measurement sets being recorded here periodically including a third set).

Claim 27 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over U.S. 2002/0143262 to Bardy in view of U.S. 2017/0007153 to Tonar et al. further in view of U.S. 2011/0191122 to Kharraz Tavakol et al. as applied to claim 22, and further in view of U.S. Patent No. 9,028,407 to Bennet-Guerrero.
As per claim 27, Bardy, Tonar et al., and Kharraz Tavakol et al. in combination teach the method of claim 21, see discussion of claim 21. Tonar et al. further teaches SEM measurements (see: paragraph [0008] where there are SEM values).
The combination fails to further, specifically teach continuing to make a plurality of measurements at a pre-determined frequency corresponding to level-K if the delta number='13'value does not exceed the threshold, and making a plurality of measurements at a pre-determined frequency corresponding to level-N if the delta value exceeds the threshold.
Bennett-Guerrero teaches continuing to make a plurality of measurements at a pre-determined frequency corresponding to level-K if the delta value does not exceed the threshold, and making a plurality of measurements at a pre-determined frequency corresponding to level-N if the delta value exceeds the threshold (see: column 6, lines 9-21 where a change in the patient’s condition changes the frequency of measurements. If there is no change in the patient’s condition then these measurements would happen a lesser frequency such as once every 10 minutes in one embodiment. A plurality of measurements at a pre-determined frequency corresponding to level-K (once every 10 minutes) is occurring and it is changed to a different predetermined frequency corresponding to level-N (once every minute in one embodiment) if the patient’s condition changes (delta value exceeds a threshold)).
One of ordinary skill at the time of the invention was filed would have found it obvious to continue to make a plurality of measurements at a pre-determined frequency corresponding to level-K if the delta value does not exceed the threshold, and making a plurality of measurements at a pre-determined frequency corresponding to level-N if the delta value exceeds the threshold as taught by Bennett-Guerrero in the method as taught by Bardy, Tonar et al., and Kharraz Tavakol et al. in combination with the motivation(s) of being beneficial for various reasons such as to enhance, improve, or even optimize battery life (see: column 6, lines 16-21 of Bennett-Guerrero).
Claims 31-32, 34, and 39 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over U.S. 2002/0143262 to Bardy in view of U.S. 2017/0007153 to Tonar et al. further in view of U.S. 2011/0191122 to Kharraz Tavakol et al. and further in view of U.S. Patent No. 6,738,798 to Ploetz et al. as applied to claim 30, and further in view of U.S. Patent No. 9,675,289 to Heaton.
As per claim 31, Bardy, Tonar et al., Kharraz Tavakol et al., and Ploetz et al. in combination teach the method of claim 29, see discussion of claim 29. Tonar et al. further teaches delta values of the at least one body location of the patient (see: paragraph [0008] where a difference value (delta value) is being determined).
The combination fails to further, specifically teach the step of:
--querying the database to retrieve a portion of data records that comprise the values.
Heaton teaches the step of:
--querying the database to retrieve a portion of data records that comprise the values (see: FIG. 9 where there is a directory for storing and retrieving archived responses into and from the database. In order for the system here to access the database here, it would query the database in order to retrieve the necessary data).
One of ordinary skill at the time of the invention was filed would have found it obvious to query the database to retrieve a portion of data records that comprise the values as taught by Heaton in the method as taught by Bardy, Tonar et al., Kharraz Tavakol et al., and Ploetz et al. in combination with the motivation(s) of being a way to number='14'view and analyze stored data in a chronological form so that trends in data may be observed.
As per claim 32, Bardy, Tonar et al., Kharraz Tavakol et al., and Ploetz et al. in combination teach the method of claim 30, see discussion of claim 30. Tonar et al. further teaches delta values (see: paragraph [0008] where a difference value (delta value) is being determined).
The combination fails to further, specifically teach the step of:
1) --formatting the retrieved values in date and time order, and
2) --displaying the formatted values.
Heaton teaches the step of:
1) --formatting the retrieved values in date and time order, (see: column 30, lines 11-31 and FIG. 8 where there are values being retrieved, formatted by time and date, and displayed on a display) and
2) --displaying the formatted values (see: column 30, lines 11-31 and FIG. 8 where there are values being retrieved, formatted by time and date, and displayed on a display).
One of ordinary skill at the time of the invention was filed would have found it obvious to 1) format the retrieved values in date and time order and 2) display the formatted values as taught by Heaton in the method as taught by Bardy, Tonar et al., Kharraz Tavakol et al., and Ploetz et al. in combination with the motivation(s) of being a way to view and analyze stored data in a chronological form so that trends in data may be observed.
As per claim 34, Bardy, Tonar et al., Kharraz Tavakol et al., Ploetz et al., and Heaton in combination teach the method of claim 32, see discussion of claim 32. Tonar et al. further teaches delta values (see: paragraph [0008] where a difference value (delta value) is being determined).
The motivations to combine the above-mentioned references are discussed in the rejection of claim 21, and incorporated herein.
Heaton further teaches wherein the formatted values is displayed in the form of a curve (see: FIG. 8).
The motivations to combine the above-mentioned references are discussed in the rejection of claim 32, and incorporated herein.
As per claim 39, Bardy, Tonar et al., Kharraz Tavakol et al., and Ploetz et al. in combination teach the method of claim 37, see discussion of claim 37. Tonar et al. further teaches delta values (see: paragraph [0008] where a difference value (delta value) is being determined).
The combination fails to further, specifically teach the step of
--querying the database to retrieve the values observed over time for a particular patient across multiple care settings and various episodes of care.
Heaton teaches the step of querying the database to retrieve the values observed over time for a particular patient across multiple care settings and various episodes of care (see: FIG. 9 where there is a directory for storing and retrieving archived responses into and from the database. In order for the system here to number='15'access the database here, it would query the database in order to retrieve the necessary data. Additionally, the data here are past data values including values across multiple care settings and care episodes. These data values are retrieved regardless of setting and care episode).
The motivations to combine the above-mentioned references are discussed in the rejection of claim 32, and incorporated herein.
Claims 31-32, 34, and 39 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over U.S. 2002/0143262 to Bardy in view of U.S. 2017/0007153 to Tonar et al. further in view of U.S. 2011/0191122 to Kharraz Tavakol et al. and further in view of U.S. Patent No. 6,738,798 to Ploetz et al. as applied to claim 30, and further in view of U.S. 2008/0015894 to Miller et al.
As per claim 33, Bardy, Tonar et al., Kharraz Tavakol et al., and Ploetz et al. in combination teach the method of claim 29, see discussion of claim 29. The combination fails to further, specifically the steps of:
--creating an additional data record that comprises the patient identifier, a data element from the group of nutritional information, an implemented intervention, a risk assessment, a visual skin assessment, a care plan, a doctor's note, lean event, a vital sign, a body weight, and a lab result, and a date/time associated with the data element, and
--reporting the additional data record to the database.
Miller et al. teaches the steps of:
number='16'--creating an additional data record that comprises the patient identifier, a data element from the group of nutritional information, an implemented intervention, a risk assessment, a visual skin assessment, a care plan, a doctor's note, lean event, a vital sign, a body weight, and a lab result, and a date/time associated with the data element, (see: paragraph [0121] where there are results being recorded in a database and these results are being considered to be the additional data record. The results can include the name of the patient (patient identifier), recommendations or changes to the therapy regimen (a care plan), as well as a date and time associated with the recommendation or change) and
--reporting the additional data record to the database (see: paragraph [0121] where the results of the contact with the medical provider are recorded with the database).
One of ordinary skill at the time of the invention was filed would have found it obvious to have the steps of creating an additional data record that comprises the patient identifier, a data element from the group of nutritional information, an implemented intervention, a risk assessment, a visual skin assessment, a care plan, a doctor's note, lean event, a vital sign, a body weight, and a lab result, and a date/time associated with the data element, and reporting the additional data record to the database as taught by Miller et al. in the method as taught by Bardy, Tonar et al., Kharraz Tavakol et al., and Ploetz et al. in combination with the motivation(s) of monitoring all relevant patient information that affect a patient’s health status so that appropriate recommendations may be made.
Claim 35 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over U.S. 2002/0143262 to Bardy in view of U.S. 2017/0007153 to Tonar et al. further in view of U.S. 2011/0191122 to Kharraz Tavakol et al. further in view of U.S. Patent No. 6,738,798 to Ploetz et al. and further in view of U.S. Patent No. 9,675,289 to Heaton, as applied to claim 32, and further in view of U.S. Patent No. 8,355,925 to Rothman et al.
As per claim 35, Bardy, Tonar et al., Kharraz Tavakol et al., Ploetz et al., and Heaton in combination teach the method of claim 32, see discussion of claim 32. Tonar et al. further teaches delta values (see: paragraph [0008] where a difference value (delta value) is being determined).
The combination fails to further, specifically teach the step of analyzing the retrieved values to determine one or more of a slope, an acceleration, a curve shape and associated characteristics, and a time-to-intercept of a selected threshold value.
Rothman et al. teaches the step of analyzing the retrieved values to determine one or more of a slope, an acceleration, a curve shape and associated characteristics, and a time-to-intercept of a selected threshold value (see: column 15, lines 29-43 where a derivative in the slope is calculated and a determination is made based on this acceleration to see if the patient is declining at a faster rate. The change in the acceleration of the slope may trigger an alarm. Also see: column 23, lines 18-29 and 51-59).
One of ordinary skill at the time of the invention was filed would have found it obvious to have the step of analyzing the retrieved values to determine one or more of a slope, an acceleration, a curve shape and associated characteristics, and a time-to-intercept of a selected threshold value as taught by Rothman et al. in the method as number='17'taught by Bardy, Tonar et al., Kharraz Tavakol et al., Ploetz et al., and Heaton in combination with the motivation(s) of alerting a user if a patient is getting better or worse at an accelerating rate (see: column 23, lines 51-59 of Rothman et al.).
